where the overbar is the complex conjugate (Chapter~\ref{ch:complex}); for complex functions the ``dot product'' conjugates the second factor. The reason for the conjugate: with it, the product of a function with itself is $\int f\bar f\,\dd x=\int|f|^2\dd x\ge0$, a genuine squared length; without it, $\int_{-L}^{L}e^{i\pi x/L}e^{i\pi x/L}\dd x$ would be $0$ (by the computation below with $k-l$ replaced by $2$) even though the function is never zero. To integrate a complex-valued function of the real variable $x$, integrate its real and imaginary parts separately: $\int(u+iv)\,\dd x=\int u\,\dd x+i\int v\,\dd x$. For a real constant $\alpha\neq0$ this gives
\[
\int e^{i\alpha x}\dd x=\int\cos\alpha x\,\dd x+i\int\sin\alpha x\,\dd x=\frac{\sin\alpha x}{\alpha}-i\frac{\cos\alpha x}{\alpha}=\frac{e^{i\alpha x}}{i\alpha},
\]
where the last step multiplies $\cos\alpha x+i\sin\alpha x$ by $1/i=-i$. So complex exponentials integrate exactly like real ones.
